It was Lokesh's fifth trip to the tehsil office in Shirdi for one stamp on his late grandfather's land mutation papers. Each time, a new reason: wrong form, missing copy, officer on leave. Today the clerk, Madhuri, said, "Come back Monday."
Lokesh felt the shout rise in his throat. He had taken another day off. His father was waiting at home.
He stepped back, breathed out slowly, and looked at her. She had a pile of files taller than her screen, and a queue of twenty behind him.
"Madam, I know it's not your fault. This is my fifth visit. Could I please speak to the supervisor?"
She pointed down the corridor. The supervisor listened, checked the file, and signed it in ten minutes.
That night Lokesh wrote down every visit, every date and reason, and submitted it on the state's online grievance portal, so the next person might need fewer trips.

qa.a: Five times; this was his fifth trip.

qa.a: He felt furious and exhausted, a shout rising in his throat after taking another day off.

qa.a: He took a breath, acknowledged it wasn't the clerk's fault, politely asked for the supervisor, and later filed a grievance online with a record of every visit.

By the third month of trying to transfer his late father's scooter to his name, Samir had stopped expecting anything from the transport office in Indore. Every visit ended the same way: a new form, a shrug. "We're just numbers to them," he told his friend Sahil over chai.
Sahil nodded. "Everyone says that. Then they pay an agent."
Samir almost agreed. He was so tired. But he thought of his mother, who had asked him to handle it so she wouldn't have to stand in those lines.
So he did something different. He downloaded the department's citizen charter, which listed every document and timeline. He printed it and went back. When the clerk asked for yet another form, he politely pointed to the charter. The transfer was done in two weeks.
Afterwards, Samir wrote a one-page guide in simple Hindi and pinned it on the notice board of his building. Three neighbours used it that month.

One Sunday morning Bao found her on the balcony, eyes red, phone in hand. "How bad?"
"Three months of rent," Aiko whispered. Her hands were shaking.
They made green tea and sat on the floor. Aiko wrote down what she'd noticed: raising the stakes after every win, betting more to win back losses, hiding it. "That's gambling," she said quietly. "Not investing."
She stopped trading that day. She set up a meeting with a registered financial counsellor, and she asked Bao to check in with her every Sunday, just to talk. Steady and boring suddenly sounded like relief.
